nameStory: The Mexican violetear gets its name from the brilliant violet-blue patches of feathers that adorn the sides of its head, looking like colorful earrings or ear tufts. These iridescent 'violet ears' flash and shimmer as the bird moves, making them one of its most distinctive features. The name perfectly captures this hummingbird's most eye-catching characteristic.
description: The Mexican violetear is a medium-sized hummingbird with stunning metallic green plumage that shimmers like emeralds in sunlight. Unlike our tiny ruby-throated hummingbirds, this species is noticeably larger and more robust. Its most striking feature is the brilliant violet-blue patches on the sides of its head that give it its name. This tropical visitor is extremely rare in New England, with only a handful of sightings ever recorded in our region.

idTips.label: Violet ear patches
idTips.description: Brilliant violet-blue feather patches on the sides of the head that flash iridescent purple and blue as the bird moves - unlike any other hummingbird you'll see in New England

idTips.label: Metallic green body
idTips.description: Entire body covered in shimmering metallic green feathers that look like polished emeralds, much more intensely green than our native ruby-throated hummingbird

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than ruby-throated hummingbirds, with a heavier, more substantial appearance in flight

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Dark, slightly forked tail with metallic green edges that catches the light - lacks the bright colors of the head and body

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Hovers at feeders with a slightly slower wingbeat than ruby-throated hummingbirds, creating a deeper buzzing sound

habitat: In New England, Mexican violetears are extremely rare vagrants that might appear at hummingbird feeders in residential areas, particularly during late summer or fall migration periods. When they do show up, it's typically in suburban gardens or parks with abundant flowering plants and established feeding stations. These birds prefer areas with some tree cover nearby for perching and protection.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen in New England during spring migration, as these birds typically follow western migration routes.
seasonality.summer: Very rare vagrant visitors might appear at hummingbird feeders, usually individual birds that have wandered far from their normal range.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely to appear during fall migration when young birds may stray from typical routes, often visiting feeders in September or October.
seasonality.winter: Does not occur in New England winters - any Mexican violetears would have continued south to warmer climates.

funFact: Mexican violetears are such strong fliers that individual birds have been known to wander over 1,000 miles from their normal range, which is how they occasionally end up at New England hummingbird feeders - making each sighting like finding a feathered lottery ticket!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with ruby-throated hummingbirds, but the Mexican violetear's violet ear patches are unmistakable - no other hummingbird in North America has this feature. Remember: if you see violet 'ears' on a hummingbird in New England, you're looking at something extremely special.
contextualKnowledge: The Mexican violetear was once considered the same species as the lesser violetear and both were called 'green violetear' - so older field guides might use this name. Any Mexican violetear spotted in New England should be reported to eBird and local birding groups, as these are exceptionally rare vagrant sightings.
compareHints: Since there are no other violetears in New England, compare this species to our common ruby-throated hummingbird. The Mexican violetear is larger, entirely metallic green (males and females), and has those distinctive violet ear patches that ruby-throats completely lack. Ruby-throated males have red throats and females have white throats - very different from the violetear's all-green appearance.
